summary.thesis: Netflix is a grade B cash generator priced for slower growth and a lower margin, but its growth is cooling and the chart has no floor yet.
summary.decision: Long-term: add a second small slice at 56.73 and hold more buying back for 52.53. Swing: no trade while the stock is in a downtrend.
summary.act_at: Add at 56.73, then at 52.53. No buying above 63.41.

note.happening: Netflix closed at 56.73, down 2.96% on the day. It sits below its 20-, 50- and 200-day averages (62.28, 67.4 and 79.94), and all three are falling. No support level is listed below the price. There is no news since the last note. Analysts cut their estimate for this quarter's earnings per share by 7.3% over 30 days, and the next report is due 2027-01-19.
note.business: The business itself has not broken. Trailing revenue is 49.7B, up from 43.4B. Free cash flow (cash left after running and investing in the business) is 11.4B, up from 9.0B. Operating margin rose to 31.3% from 29.14%, and the share count fell 3.35% in a year, so each share owns more of the company. What is at risk is the pace: quarterly sales growth slowed to 11.85% from 16.19% two quarters earlier. The filings also say the 31% margin sits at the top of its 5-year range (17–31%), and peaks like that usually fade. The balance sheet is not at risk, though it is not spotless: debt of 12.7B against cash of 8.2B leaves net debt of 4.4B, which cash flow of 11.4B covers easily. Today's fall, the downtrend and the estimate cuts are mostly about sentiment. They do not yet show weaker demand or cash generation.

worth.text: The stock trades at 16.1 times trailing earnings and 15.0 times next year's estimate. It trades at 4.7 times sales, against a peer median of 6.8 and at the 18th percentile of its own 5-year range. A cash-flow model (DCF, which values a company by the future cash it is expected to produce) gives 37.39 in the bear case, 63.41 in the base case and 75.66 in the bull case. Its own past price-to-sales range gives 58.94 to 122.15. The gap between the two methods comes from growth. The history method assumes investors will pay the multiples they paid in faster-growth years. The DCF only pays for cash flow. The price implies free cash flow growth of about 11.9% at the start. At 10% growth the model gives 52.53, and at 20% it gives 78.35. If operating margin fell to 23%, the value would be 58.49, which is above today's price. So the price already allows for a meaningful margin fade. A deeper fall to 15% would give 38.63.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow starts growing at 10% to 20% a year, close to the 11.9% the price implies, and operating margin does not fall much below 23%.
